<reason>A genuinely close debate between two strong, disciplined cases. B built the more intuitive harm story (wasted comparison effort, the late-arriving family) and answered both pressure questions directly and honestly. But A won the key micro-clashes: (1) B's "where law complies, nothing changes" response effectively conceded the motion's fee half adds little, narrowing PRO's case to house rules; (2) A's answer to B's best pressure question — that a legal display duty converts omission from an unenforceability risk into a violation, driving defensive completeness ("curation into coverage") — survived, while B's closing response mischaracterized it as being about "inventing" restrictions, which A cleanly exposed with the last word; (3) A resolved B's "routine vs. disruptive" catch sharply (fees routine hence redundant; rules new hence disruptive). A's marginal-benefit-near-zero vs. certain-marginal-cost weighing gave the cleaner decision rule, while B's strongest surviving point ("incentive ≠ guarantee") only showed a sliver of residual harm without restoring the motion's breadth. Grounding was good on both sides; A's regulatory references were accurate and appropriately hedged.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's A1 in Rebuttal 2: answering B's challenge that checkout terms are already enforceable, A distinguished commercial unenforceability from statutory violation as the actual inflation driver — rescuing the boilerplate mechanism that carried CON's cost case, and B never squarely re-engaged that distinction.</best_rebuttal>
